title: Equation Atlas
note: Every calculator output is computed from 'expr' (JavaScript, SI units) using the constants below. Inputs are in display units; 'mul' converts to SI and output 'div' converts back. Verified by scripts/check_equations.mjs.

chapters.title: Gravity & Orbits
chapters.blurb: One inverse-square law, three laws of Kepler, and the handful of formulas every mission designer carries in their head: how fast, how long, how far, and how much velocity change (Δv) it costs to go somewhere else.

chapters.title: Rockets
chapters.blurb: A rocket is a machine for throwing mass backwards very fast. These equations say how much speed that buys, why we build rockets in stages, and what the atmosphere and gravity take back on the way up.

chapters.title: Atmosphere & Re-entry
chapters.blurb: Air thins exponentially with height, sound has a speed limit, and a capsule coming home at 11 km/s turns its kinetic energy into a shock layer hotter than the surface of the Sun.

chapters.title: Light & Stars
chapters.blurb: Almost everything we know about stars arrives as light. Temperature sets the colour, size and temperature set the power, distance dims it, and motion shifts it.

chapters.title: Relativity & Black Holes
chapters.blurb: Moving clocks run slow, clocks deep in gravity run slower, and enough mass in a small enough space closes off a region of spacetime entirely. Satellite navigation depends on all of it.

chapters.title: Cosmology
chapters.blurb: The Universe is expanding. A few equations connect the redshift of distant galaxies to the size, age, density and temperature of the whole cosmos.

equations.title: Newton's law of universal gravitation

legend.desc: Attractive force between the two bodies

equations.meaning: Every mass pulls on every other mass along the line joining them. Double either mass and the pull doubles; double the distance and it falls to a quarter. The same law drops an apple, holds the Moon in orbit and shapes galaxies. Isaac Newton published it in the Principia (1687).

example.title: How hard do the Earth and Moon pull on each other?
example.text: Earth $m_1 = 5.972\times10^{24}$ kg, Moon $m_2 = 7.346\times10^{22}$ kg, mean separation $r = 384\,400$ km.

answer.text: about 20 billion billion newtons — enough to raise tides of metres in the oceans.

plot.caption: Force against distance: a straight line of slope −2 on log–log axes.

refs.label: NASA/JPL — Basics of Space Flight, Chapter 3: Gravity & Mechanics
Wikipedia — Newton's law of universal gravitation

equations.title: Kepler's first law — orbits are ellipses

legend.desc: Distance from the focus (the Sun) to the planet
Semi-major axis (half the long axis of the ellipse)
Eccentricity: 0 is a circle, close to 1 is a long thin ellipse
True anomaly: angle from the closest point (periapsis)

equations.meaning: Planets do not move in circles. Johannes Kepler found in 1609, from Tycho Brahe's observations of Mars, that each orbit is an ellipse with the Sun at one focus — not at the centre. The closest point is $r_p = a(1-e)$ (perihelion) and the farthest is $r_a = a(1+e)$ (aphelion).

example.title: How close does Mars get to the Sun?

answer.text: about 206.7 million km; at aphelion Mars is 1.666 AU away — a 21 % swing.

plot.caption: The ellipse with the Sun at one focus; drag the anomaly slider to move the planet.

refs.label: NASA Science — Orbits and Kepler's Laws
Wikipedia — Kepler's laws of planetary motion

equations.title: Kepler's second law — equal areas in equal times

legend.desc: Area swept per second by the Sun–planet line
Gravitational parameter of the central body

equations.meaning: A line from the Sun to a planet sweeps out equal areas in equal times. Close to the Sun the line is short, so the planet must move fast; far away it crawls. Physically this is conservation of angular momentum, and it gives the speed ratio $v_p/v_a = (1+e)/(1-e)$ between perihelion and aphelion.

example.title: How much faster is Earth in January than in July?

answer.text: at perihelion (early January) versus 29.29 km/s at aphelion (early July) — 3.4 % faster.

plot.caption: Twelve wedges, each swept in the same time. The planet moves at its true Keplerian speed.

refs.label: NASA Science — Orbits and Kepler's Laws
Wikipedia — Kepler's laws of planetary motion

equations.title: Kepler's third law — the harmonic law

legend.desc: Central mass and orbiting mass (here $m \ll M$ is neglected)

equations.meaning: The square of a planet's year is proportional to the cube of its orbit size. In units of years and astronomical units (AU) around the Sun it collapses to $T^2 = a^3$. Newton showed where the constant comes from, which turns the law into a scale: measure an orbit and you have weighed the central body.

example.title: How long is a year on Mars?
example.text: Mars orbits at $a = 1.5237$ AU around a Sun of $1\,M_\odot$. In solar units $T = a^{3/2}$ years:

answer.text: that is 687 Earth days.

plot.caption: The eight planets (dots, NASA planetary fact sheets) sit on the line T ∝ a^1.5.

refs.label: NASA Science — Orbits and Kepler's Laws
Wikipedia — Kepler's laws of planetary motion

equations.title: Vis-viva equation

legend.desc: Standard gravitational parameter of the central body
Current distance from the centre of the central body

equations.meaning: The single most useful equation in orbital mechanics. It is conservation of energy for an orbit: kinetic plus potential energy per kilogram is fixed by the orbit's size, $-\mu/2a$. Know where you are ($r$) and which orbit you are on ($a$) and you know your speed. A circle ($r = a$) and an escape trajectory ($a \to \infty$) are special cases.

example.title: Speed at the low point of a geostationary transfer orbit (GTO)
example.text: Perigee at 200 km altitude ($r = 6\,578$ km), apogee at geostationary radius (42 164 km), so $a = 24\,371$ km.

answer.text: about 2.45 km/s faster than a circular orbit at the same height (7.78 km/s).

outputs.label: Orbital speed
outputs.hint: — means r > 2a: that point is not on this orbit

plot.caption: Speed along the orbit (bright) against circular and escape speed at the same radius.

refs.label: R. A. Braeunig — Rocket & Space Technology: Orbital Mechanics

equations.title: Orbital period

legend.desc: Semi-major axis (orbit radius for a circle)
Gravitational parameter of the central body

equations.meaning: Kepler's third law written for satellites. The period depends only on the size of the orbit, not on its shape or on the satellite's mass. That is why every satellite at 35 786 km altitude takes one sidereal day (23 h 56 min) and appears to hang still over the equator.

example.title: How long does the International Space Station (ISS) take to lap Earth?
example.text: The ISS flies about 420 km above Earth's mean radius of 6 371 km, so $a \approx 6\,791$ km.

answer.text: ≈ 92.8 minutes — about 15.5 orbits and 16 sunrises a day.

plot.caption: Period (hours) against orbit size.

refs.label: NASA/JPL — Basics of Space Flight, Chapter 3: Gravity & Mechanics

equations.title: Circular orbital velocity

legend.desc: Speed needed for a circular orbit
Orbit radius from the body's centre

equations.meaning: In a circular orbit gravity supplies exactly the centripetal force: $GMm/r^2 = mv^2/r$. The spacecraft is always falling, but it moves sideways fast enough that the ground curves away beneath it just as fast. Higher orbits are slower.

example.title: How fast is the ISS moving?

answer.text: about 27 600 km/h — London to New York in 12 minutes.

plot.caption: Higher orbits are slower: v ∝ r^−½.

refs.label: NASA/JPL — Basics of Space Flight, Chapter 3: Gravity & Mechanics

equations.title: Escape velocity

legend.desc: Speed at which kinetic energy equals the depth of the gravity well

equations.meaning: Throw something at this speed (ignoring air) and it coasts away forever, slowing down but never quite stopping. Set kinetic energy $\tfrac12 v^2$ equal to the gravitational binding energy $\mu/r$. It is always exactly $\sqrt2 \approx 1.414$ times the circular speed at the same radius.

example.title: Escape velocity from Earth's surface

answer.text: roughly 40 000 km/h. From the Moon's surface it is only 2.38 km/s.

plot.caption: Escape speed (bright) is always √2 × circular speed.

refs.label: NASA/JPL — Basics of Space Flight, Chapter 3: Gravity & Mechanics

equations.title: Hohmann transfer Δv

legend.desc: Radii of the starting and target circular orbits
Gravitational parameter of the central body
Transfer time (half the transfer ellipse's period)

equations.meaning: Walter Hohmann showed in 1925 that the cheapest two-burn route between circular orbits is half an ellipse that just touches both. Burn prograde to stretch the orbit, coast half an orbit, burn again to circularise. It is slow but fuel-efficient, and it is how most satellites reach geostationary orbit and how Mars missions are timed.

example.title: Low Earth orbit (LEO) to geostationary orbit (GEO)
example.text: From a 300 km circular orbit ($r_1 = 6\,678$ km) to GEO ($r_2 = 42\,164$ km).

answer.text: 2.43 + 1.47 km/s, with a 5.3-hour coast. (A real GEO transfer also changes inclination, which costs more.)

plot.caption: Inner and outer circular orbits with the half-ellipse transfer; burns shown as arrows.

refs.label: R. A. Braeunig — Rocket & Space Technology: Orbital Mechanics

equations.title: Sphere of influence

legend.desc: Radius of the planet's sphere of influence (SOI)
Planet's orbital distance from the larger body
Mass of the planet and of the body it orbits

equations.meaning: Inside this radius it is more accurate to treat a spacecraft as orbiting the planet (with the Sun as a small disturbance); outside, as orbiting the Sun. Mission designers use it to stitch simple two-body orbits together — the 'patched conic' method used to plan the Apollo and Voyager trajectories.

example.title: Earth's sphere of influence

answer.text: about 2.4 times the Moon's distance.

plot.caption: SOI radius against planet mass at the chosen distance.

refs.label: R. A. Braeunig — Rocket & Space Technology: Orbital Mechanics

equations.title: Hill sphere

legend.desc: Hill radius: where the planet's gravity dominates the tidal pull of the star

equations.meaning: A moon must orbit well inside this radius to stay bound to its planet; in practice stable moons live within about a third to a half of $r_H$. It is set by the balance of the planet's gravity against the star's tidal stretching, which is why the cube root appears. The Sun–Earth L1 and L2 points sit almost exactly on it.

example.title: Earth's Hill sphere

answer.text: about 1.47 million km; the Moon, at 0.38 million km, is comfortably inside.

plot.caption: Hill radius grows only as the cube root of the planet's mass.

refs.label: NASA Science — What is a Lagrange Point?

equations.title: Roche limit

legend.desc: Closest distance (centre to centre) a moon can orbit without being torn apart
Radius of the primary (planet or star)
Mean densities of the primary and the satellite

equations.meaning: Closer than this, the difference in the planet's pull across a moon (the tide) beats the moon's own gravity, and a moon held together only by gravity comes apart. Édouard Roche computed it in 1848. A rigid body survives closer in; a fluid rubble pile breaks up farther out. Saturn's bright rings lie inside Saturn's Roche limit, and comet Shoemaker–Levy 9 was shredded passing inside Jupiter's in 1992.

example.title: How close could the Moon come to Earth?

answer.text: about 18 400 km (rigid-body limit 9 490 km). Today the Moon is 21 times farther away.

plot.caption: Fluid (bright) and rigid limits against satellite density: fluffier moons break up farther out.

equations.title: L1 / L2 Lagrange-point distance

legend.desc: Distance of L1 (or L2) from the smaller body

equations.meaning: L1 and L2 are the two points on the line through a star and planet where a spacecraft can orbit the star in lock-step with the planet: gravity and the rotating frame's centrifugal effect balance. For a small mass ratio both sit about one Hill radius from the planet. The Solar and Heliospheric Observatory (SOHO) watches the Sun from Sun–Earth L1; the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) hides from it at L2.

example.title: How far away is JWST's home, Sun–Earth L2?

answer.text: about 1.5 million km — four times farther than the Moon. (The approximation errs by about 1 % here.)

plot.caption: L1/L2 distance against the smaller body's mass.

refs.label: NASA Science — What is a Lagrange Point?

equations.title: Tsiolkovsky rocket equation

legend.desc: Change in velocity the rocket can achieve (no gravity or drag)

equations.meaning: Konstantin Tsiolkovsky published this in 1903 and it rules all of rocketry. Because each kilogram of propellant must also accelerate the propellant still on board, Δv grows only with the logarithm of the mass ratio. Doubling Δv means squaring the mass ratio — the 'tyranny of the rocket equation'.

example.title: A hydrogen–oxygen stage with a mass ratio of 4
example.text: An RS-25-class engine in vacuum ($I_{sp} = 452$ s) on a stage that is 75 % propellant ($m_0/m_f = 4$).

answer.text: about two-thirds of what it takes to reach low Earth orbit (≈ 9.4 km/s including losses).

plot.caption: Δv against mass ratio; dim curves for solid (268 s) and kerosene (311 s) engines. Note the diminishing returns.

refs.label: NASA Glenn Research Center — Ideal Rocket Equation

equations.title: Rocket thrust equation

legend.desc: Exhaust velocity at the nozzle exit
Exhaust pressure at the nozzle exit, and ambient pressure

equations.meaning: Thrust has two parts. The big one is momentum: mass thrown back each second times its speed. The second is a pressure imbalance across the nozzle exit. At sea level the air pushes back on an engine designed for altitude ($p_a > p_e$), so the same engine gains thrust as it climbs into thinner air.

example.title: An F-1-class engine at sea level (illustrative round numbers)

answer.text: about 6.76 MN; the pressure term costs 338 kN at sea level and becomes a bonus of 756 kN in vacuum. (The real F-1 made about 6.77 MN at sea level.)

plot.caption: Thrust rises as the ambient pressure falls away during the climb.

refs.label: NASA Glenn Research Center — Rocket Thrust Equation

equations.title: Specific impulse and effective exhaust velocity

legend.desc: Specific impulse: seconds a unit weight of propellant can produce thrust equal to its weight
Standard gravity (a unit convention, not local gravity)

equations.meaning: Specific impulse is the 'miles per gallon' of a rocket engine: thrust per unit of propellant flow. Multiply by $g_0$ and you get the effective exhaust velocity that goes straight into the rocket equation. Chemical engines top out near 450 s; electric thrusters reach thousands of seconds but with tiny thrust.

example.title: The Space Shuttle Main Engine (RS-25) in vacuum
example.text: Thrust about $2\,279$ kN with a propellant flow of about $514$ kg/s.

answer.text: matching the published ≈ 452 s; exhaust velocity ≈ 4.43 km/s.

plot.caption: Your engine (bright) against real engines, published vacuum values.

refs.label: NASA Glenn Research Center — Specific Impulse

equations.title: Mass ratio and propellant fraction
equations.aka: How much of a rocket is fuel

legend.desc: Final mass: structure, engines, upper stages and payload

equations.meaning: Two ways to say the same thing. The mass ratio goes into the logarithm of the rocket equation; the propellant fraction says how much of the vehicle is fuel. Orbital rockets are over 85 % propellant at liftoff — proportionally less 'container' than an egg's shell.

example.title: The Saturn V first-stage (S-IC) burn
example.text: S-IC propellant ≈ 2 077 t. Everything left at burnout — the empty S-IC (137 t) plus the fuelled upper stages and Apollo spacecraft — ≈ 771 t.

answer.text: so ζ ≈ 72.9 % of the whole stack was burned in the first 2½ minutes.

plot.caption: Mass ratio against propellant load for the chosen burnout mass.

refs.label: NASA Glenn Research Center — Mass Ratios

equations.title: Multi-stage Δv

legend.desc: Ideal velocity change of the whole vehicle
Mass when stage $i$ ignites (it and everything above it)
Mass when stage $i$ burns out, $m_{0,i} - m_{p,i}$

equations.meaning: Staging beats the rocket equation by throwing away empty tanks and heavy engines as soon as they stop being useful. Each stage runs the rocket equation on a lighter vehicle, and the Δv values simply add. That is why every orbital launcher so far has used at least two stages.

example.title: Saturn V: pad to the Moon
example.text: Payload (Apollo spacecraft) 43.5 t. S-IC: 2 077 t propellant, 137 t dry, $I_{sp}\approx 283$ s averaged over the climb. S-II: 427 t / 43 t, 424 s. S-IVB: 105.3 t / 15.2 t, 424 s (rounded published figures).

answer.text: ideal (3.63 + 4.65 + 4.27 km/s): enough for ≈ 9.4 km/s to orbit including gravity and drag losses, plus ≈ 3.1 km/s for trans-lunar injection.

plot.caption: Each stage's contribution to the ideal Δv (km/s).

equations.title: Drag equation

legend.desc: Drag force opposing motion through the air
Drag coefficient (shape; varies with Mach number)

equations.meaning: Drag grows with the square of speed and in direct proportion to air density. Launch vehicles are slim and pointed to keep $C_D A$ small and climb out of the dense lower air before going fast. Capsules do the opposite on the way home: blunt, high-drag shapes that shed speed high up.

example.title: A 3.66 m-diameter rocket at 10 km altitude
example.text: Air density at 10 km $\rho = 0.4135$ kg/m³ (U.S. Standard Atmosphere 1976), $v = 500$ m/s, $C_D = 0.3$ (illustrative), $A = \pi(1.83)^2 = 10.52$ m².

answer.text: about 16.6 tonnes-force pushing back on the vehicle.

plot.caption: Drag grows with the square of speed.

refs.label: NASA Glenn Research Center — Drag Equation

equations.title: Dynamic pressure and Max-Q

legend.desc: Dynamic pressure: the kinetic energy per unit volume of the oncoming air
Density scale height, here 8.5 km (simple exponential model)

equations.meaning: During launch the rocket speeds up while the air thins out, so $q$ rises, peaks and falls. That peak is 'Max-Q', the moment of greatest aerodynamic stress, typically about a minute after liftoff at 10–14 km. Many rockets throttle down through it — a 'throttle bucket'.

example.title: A typical Max-Q
example.text: Altitude $h = 11$ km, speed $v = 420$ m/s, exponential atmosphere.

answer.text: about 30 kPa, the same order as the Space Shuttle's Max-Q of ≈ 35 kPa.

plot.caption: q against altitude at your speed (bright) and at 300 and 600 m/s.

refs.label: NASA Glenn Research Center — Dynamic Pressure

equations.title: Gravity loss

legend.desc: Velocity lost to gravity during the burn
Flight-path angle above the horizon ($90^\circ$ = straight up)

equations.meaning: Every second a rocket spends climbing, gravity steals $g\sin\gamma$ metres per second of the velocity its engines produce. Burning faster (a higher thrust-to-weight ratio) and pitching over towards horizontal sooner both cut the loss — but pitching over too early means more drag in dense air. Real launches lose roughly 1–1.5 km/s this way.

example.title: A first-stage burn
example.text: 150 s burn at $g = 9.81$ m/s² with an average flight-path angle of 50°.

answer.text: over a kilometre per second that the engines had to supply but that never became speed.

plot.caption: Loss against average flight-path angle: steep climbs pay the most.

refs.label: R. A. Braeunig — Rocket & Space Technology: Orbital Mechanics

equations.title: Barometric formula and scale height

legend.desc: Pressure at height $h$ and at the surface
Scale height: climb by $H$ and pressure falls by a factor $e \approx 2.718$
Molar gas constant, 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹

equations.meaning: Each layer of air is squashed by the weight of all the air above it, which makes pressure fall off exponentially. A warm atmosphere of light gas on a low-gravity world is puffy (large $H$); a cold, heavy one on a massive planet hugs the ground. Earth's scale height is about 8 km.

example.title: Air pressure on the summit of Everest

answer.text: about a third of sea-level pressure (measured ≈ 34 kPa — the real atmosphere is colder aloft).

plot.caption: Pressure on a log scale is a straight line: an exponential fall-off.

equations.title: Speed of sound and Mach number
equations.aka: Acoustic speed in an ideal gas

legend.desc: Ratio of specific heats (1.40 for air, ≈ 1.29 for CO₂)
Mach number, speed as a multiple of $a$

equations.meaning: Sound is a pressure wave carried by molecules bumping into each other, so it travels at roughly the speed of those molecules — which depends only on temperature and molecular mass, not on pressure. Above Mach 1 the air ahead cannot 'hear' you coming, and shock waves form.

example.title: Concorde at cruise
example.text: In the stratosphere $T = 216.65$ K. Concorde cruised near $v = 600$ m/s.

answer.text: Mach 2 — twice the local speed of sound.

plot.caption: Speed of sound grows as √T.

refs.label: NASA Glenn Research Center — Speed of Sound
NASA Glenn Research Center — Role of the Mach Number

equations.title: Stagnation temperature

legend.desc: Stagnation (total) temperature: air brought to rest against the vehicle
Static temperature of the free air

equations.meaning: When fast-moving air is slowed to a stop on a nose or leading edge, its kinetic energy turns back into heat. The temperature rise grows with the square of the Mach number, which is why supersonic aircraft need heat-resistant skins. For true re-entry speeds the formula over-predicts, because the air molecules break apart and absorb energy.

example.title: The SR-71 Blackbird at Mach 3.2

answer.text: about 387 °C — the aircraft's titanium skin got hot enough to stretch in flight.

plot.caption: Stagnation temperature against Mach number (ideal gas).

refs.label: NASA Glenn Research Center — Stagnation Temperature
NASA Glenn Research Center — Isentropic Flow Equations

equations.title: Sutton–Graves stagnation-point heat flux

legend.desc: Convective heat flux at the stagnation point (the nose)
Atmosphere constant: $1.7415\times10^{-4}$ for Earth, $1.9027\times10^{-4}$ for Mars

equations.meaning: Kenneth Sutton and Randolph Graves (NASA Langley, 1971) fitted this to detailed boundary-layer calculations. Heating grows with the cube of speed, so a lunar return at 11 km/s heats the nose about 3.4 times as hard as a return from orbit at 7.5 km/s. It also explains the blunt-body idea: a bigger nose radius means less heat flux, which is why capsules are wide and rounded, not pointed.

example.title: An Apollo-style lunar return
example.text: At about 60 km altitude $\rho = 3.1\times10^{-4}$ kg/m³, speed 11 km/s, heat-shield radius of curvature $R_n = 4.69$ m.

answer.text: about 1.9 MW per square metre from convection alone (at lunar-return speeds, radiation from the hot shock layer adds more).

plot.caption: Heat flux climbs with the cube of speed.

refs.label: Sutton & Graves (1971), NASA TR R-376 (NASA Technical Reports Server)

equations.title: Ballistic coefficient
equations.meaning: One number that says how easily the atmosphere slows a falling object. Low $\beta$ (light and draggy: a capsule, a parachute) decelerates high in thin air where heating is gentler; high $\beta$ (dense and slim: a meteorite, a warhead) punches deep before slowing. Entry, descent and landing designers juggle it against heat-shield mass.

example.title: The Apollo command module
example.text: Entry mass ≈ 5 560 kg, diameter 3.9 m ($A = 11.95$ m²), $C_D \approx 1.3$ (illustrative).

answer.text: kg/m²; at 60 km and 11 km/s that means about 5.3 g of deceleration.

plot.caption: Deceleration (in g) against air density at the chosen speed.

equations.title: Stefan–Boltzmann law
equations.meaning: Each square metre of a hot surface radiates $\sigma T^4$ watts, so doubling the temperature multiplies the power by sixteen. Multiply by the surface area of a sphere and you have a star's total output. This is how astronomers estimate the sizes of stars they can never resolve: measure $L$ and $T$, solve for $R$.

example.title: The Sun's power output

answer.text: watts — the IAU nominal solar luminosity.

plot.caption: Luminosity against temperature for your radius (bright) and for 0.1, 10 and 100 R☉.

refs.label: OpenStax University Physics III §6.2 — Blackbody Radiation (LibreTexts)
Prša et al. — IAU 2015 Resolution B3 (nominal solar & planetary constants)

equations.title: Wien's displacement law

legend.desc: Wavelength at which the blackbody spectrum peaks

equations.meaning: Hotter objects glow at shorter wavelengths. A stove ring goes from dull red to orange as it heats; stars run from red (cool) through yellow and white to blue (hot). One division gives a star's temperature from its colour, a person's glow in the thermal infrared, or the microwave peak of the Big Bang's afterglow.

example.title: Where does sunlight peak?

answer.text: nm — blue-green, right in the middle of the band our eyes evolved to see.

plot.caption: Peak wavelength against temperature; the shaded band is visible light.

refs.label: OpenStax University Physics III §6.2 — Blackbody Radiation (LibreTexts)

equations.title: Planck's law

legend.desc: Spectral radiance: power per area, per solid angle, per wavelength
Planck constant, speed of light, Boltzmann constant

equations.meaning: Max Planck's 1900 formula for the full spectrum of a hot object — the first equation of quantum physics. It assumes light is emitted in packets of energy $hc/\lambda$, which suppresses the short-wavelength end and cured the 'ultraviolet catastrophe'. Integrate it and you get the Stefan–Boltzmann law; find its peak and you get Wien's law.

example.title: The Sun's spectrum at 500 nm
example.text: $T = 5\,772$ K, $\lambda = 500$ nm. The exponent is $hc/\lambda k_B T = 4.985$.

answer.text: kW per square metre per steradian per nanometre, near the top of the curve.

plot.caption: Planck curves: your temperature (bright) against 3 500 K, 5 772 K and 8 000 K. Toggle a log axis to compare them.

refs.label: OpenStax University Physics III §6.2 — Blackbody Radiation (LibreTexts)

equations.title: Inverse-square law of flux

legend.desc: Flux: power per unit area arriving at distance $d$

equations.meaning: A star's light spreads over an ever-larger sphere, whose area grows as $d^2$. Twice as far, a quarter of the light. This sets the solar power available to spacecraft (why missions beyond Jupiter use nuclear power), the temperature of planets, and — with a known luminosity — the distance to a star.

example.title: The solar constant at Earth

answer.text: W/m² — what satellites measure above the atmosphere (≈ 1 361 W/m²).

plot.caption: Flux against distance, with planets marked on the curve.

refs.label: Prša et al. — IAU 2015 Resolution B3 (nominal solar & planetary constants)

equations.title: Apparent magnitude and distance modulus

legend.desc: Apparent magnitude (how bright it looks; smaller is brighter)
Absolute magnitude (how bright it would look from 10 parsecs)

equations.meaning: Astronomers still use the ancient Greek scale, made precise by Norman Pogson in 1856: 5 magnitudes is exactly a factor of 100 in brightness, and bigger numbers are fainter. The distance modulus $m - M$ is the inverse-square law in magnitude form: compare how bright a star looks with how bright it really is, and you get its distance.

example.title: How bright is the Sun in our sky?

answer.text: about 13 billion times brighter than Sirius (m = −1.46).

plot.caption: Apparent magnitude against distance (brighter is up).

refs.label: OpenStax Astronomy 2e §17.4 — Using spectra to measure stellar radius, composition, and motion

equations.title: Doppler shift

legend.desc: Radial speed as a fraction of light speed (positive = receding)

equations.meaning: Light from a source moving away is stretched to longer, redder wavelengths; from one approaching, squeezed bluer. Measuring the shift of known spectral lines gives a star's speed towards or away from us. Tiny periodic shifts of a few metres per second revealed the first exoplanet around a Sun-like star, 51 Pegasi b, in 1995.

example.title: Hydrogen-alpha from a star receding at 30 km/s
example.text: Rest wavelength of the H-alpha line: 656.28 nm.

answer.text: nm — a shift of one part in 10 000, easily measured by a spectrograph.

plot.caption: Relativistic redshift (bright) versus the classical v/c (dim): they part company above ~0.1 c.

equations.title: Parallax distance

legend.desc: Parallax angle: half the star's apparent shift over a year

equations.meaning: As Earth circles the Sun, nearby stars appear to shift back and forth against distant ones. The bigger the wobble, the closer the star. A star with a parallax of one arcsecond is one parsec away (3.26 light-years) — that is the definition of the parsec. The European Space Agency's (ESA) Gaia mission has measured parallaxes of more than a billion stars.

example.title: Distance to Proxima Centauri, our nearest star

answer.text: pc = 4.25 light-years = 268 500 AU.

plot.caption: Distance (light-years) against parallax.

refs.label: ESA Science & Technology — Measuring stellar distances by parallax

equations.title: Mass–luminosity relation

legend.desc: Luminosity in units of the Sun's
Mass in units of the Sun's

equations.meaning: For stars fusing hydrogen in their cores (the main sequence), luminosity climbs steeply with mass: a star twice the Sun's mass is about sixteen times brighter. Since fuel only grows in proportion to mass, massive stars burn out in a few million years while red dwarfs will shine for trillions. This is an empirical fit, good to tens of per cent.

example.title: Alpha Centauri A

answer.text: L☉, close to the measured ≈ 1.5 L☉, with a main-sequence life of about 7.5 billion years.

plot.caption: The fitted relation with measured stars (dots).

equations.title: Eddington luminosity

legend.desc: Luminosity at which radiation pressure balances gravity
Mass of the star or black hole

equations.meaning: Light pushes. Shine too brightly and the outward push of photons on electrons (which drag protons with them) beats gravity's pull, blowing gas away. Arthur Eddington derived this ceiling in the 1920s. It caps how bright a star can be and how fast a black hole can swallow gas — the brightest quasars shine near it.

example.title: The Eddington limit of the Sun

answer.text: W ≈ 33 000 L☉. The Sun shines at only 0.003 % of its limit.

plot.caption: The limit grows in direct proportion to mass.

equations.title: Lorentz factor

legend.desc: Lorentz factor (1 at rest, infinite at light speed)
Speed of light in vacuum, 299 792 458 m/s (exact)

equations.meaning: The one number behind special relativity: moving clocks tick slow by $\gamma$, moving rulers shrink by $\gamma$, and kinetic energy is $(\gamma - 1)mc^2$. It stays within a whisker of 1 at everyday and even spaceflight speeds, then shoots to infinity as $v \to c$ — which is why nothing with mass reaches light speed.

example.title: A spaceship at 90 % of light speed

answer.text: one year aboard is 2.29 years for the people back home.

plot.caption: γ is flat for most speeds, then explodes near c.

equations.title: Special-relativistic time dilation

legend.desc: Time elapsed for the stay-at-home observer
Proper time elapsed on the moving clock

equations.meaning: A clock moving relative to you ticks slower, by the factor $\gamma$. At everyday speeds the effect is tiny but real: atomic clocks flown around the world (Hafele and Keating, 1971) and clocks in orbit confirm it. Astronauts come home very slightly younger than they would otherwise be.

example.title: Scott Kelly's Year in Space
example.text: 340 days aboard the ISS at $v \approx 7.66$ km/s (special-relativistic part only; the gravitational effect partly offsets it).

answer.text: about 9.6 milliseconds younger than his twin, from speed alone.

plot.caption: γ − 1 against speed: it grows as v² until close to c.

refs.label: Ashby (2003), Relativity in the Global Positioning System — Living Reviews in Relativity

equations.title: Mass–energy equivalence
equations.meaning: Albert Einstein's 1905 result: mass is a form of energy, and $c^2$ (about $9\times10^{16}$) is the exchange rate. Nuclear reactions release energy by converting a small fraction of mass — the Sun turns about 4 million tonnes of mass into sunlight every second, and a fusion reaction converts about 0.7 % of the hydrogen's mass.

example.title: The energy in one gram of matter

answer.text: joules ≈ 21.5 kilotons of TNT — more than the Hiroshima bomb (≈ 15 kt).

equations.title: Schwarzschild radius
equations.aka: Event-horizon radius of a non-rotating black hole

legend.desc: Gravitational constant and speed of light

equations.meaning: Karl Schwarzschild found this in 1916, weeks after Einstein published general relativity. Squeeze any mass inside this radius and not even light can climb out. It is also the radius at which the Newtonian escape velocity would equal $c$. It scales linearly with mass: about 3 km per solar mass.

example.title: If the Sun were a black hole

answer.text: km — the whole Sun crushed to the size of a small town.

plot.caption: Horizon size is directly proportional to mass.

refs.label: A. Hamilton (JILA, University of Colorado) — More about the Schwarzschild geometry

equations.title: Gravitational time dilation and redshift
equations.aka: Clocks run slow in a gravity well

legend.desc: Rate of a clock at radius $r$ compared with one far away
Gravitational redshift of light climbing out to infinity

equations.meaning: In general relativity, clocks deeper in a gravitational well tick more slowly, and light climbing out loses energy and reddens. On Earth's surface the effect is about 60 microseconds per day relative to deep space; at a neutron star's surface clocks run 20 % slow; at the event horizon of a black hole they appear to stop.

example.title: The surface of a neutron star

answer.text: so surface clocks run at 81 % of the rate of distant clocks, and X-ray lines arrive 24 % redder.

outputs.label: Gravitational redshift
outputs.hint: — means r is inside the horizon

plot.caption: Clock rate from the horizon (0) out to 60 horizon radii.

refs.label: Ashby (2003), Relativity in the Global Positioning System — Living Reviews in Relativity

equations.title: Hawking temperature

legend.desc: Temperature of the black hole's thermal radiation
Time to evaporate completely (photons only, idealised)

equations.meaning: Stephen Hawking showed in 1974 that quantum effects make black holes glow faintly, like a blackbody. Bigger black holes are colder: a stellar-mass one is far colder than the 2.7 K cosmic background, so today it absorbs more than it emits. Only tiny black holes would be hot enough to evaporate within the age of the Universe.

example.title: A black hole with the mass of the Sun

answer.text: K — sixty billionths of a kelvin, with an evaporation time of about 10⁶⁷ years.

plot.caption: Hawking temperature against mass; above the line a black hole is hotter than the cosmic background.

equations.title: GPS clock correction

legend.desc: Fractional rate difference, orbiting clock minus ground clock
Orbit radius and orbital speed of the satellite

equations.meaning: Global Positioning System (GPS) clocks sit higher in Earth's gravity well, so general relativity makes them run fast by about 45.7 μs a day; their orbital speed makes them run slow by about 7.2 μs a day. The net is about +38 μs/day. Light travels 11 km in 38 μs, so without correction positions would drift by kilometres every day. The satellite clocks are deliberately tuned slightly slow before launch.

example.title: A GPS satellite
example.text: Orbit radius $r = 26\,562$ km, ground clock at $R_\oplus = 6\,371$ km.

answer.text: μs per day fast (45.72 from gravity − 7.21 from speed), ≈ 11.5 km of ranging error per day if ignored.

plot.caption: Net (bright), gravity and speed terms against orbit radius. Below 1.5 R⊕ orbiting clocks run slow.

refs.label: Ashby (2003), Relativity in the Global Positioning System — Living Reviews in Relativity

equations.title: Hubble–Lemaître law
equations.aka: Recession velocity and the Hubble time

legend.desc: Hubble time: a rough age scale of the Universe

equations.meaning: Georges Lemaître (1927) and Edwin Hubble (1929) found that galaxies recede at speeds proportional to their distance — the signature of a uniformly expanding Universe. Early-Universe measurements (Planck: 67.4) and nearby supernova distances (SH0ES: ≈ 73) disagree slightly; that 'Hubble tension' is one of cosmology's open problems.

example.title: A galaxy 100 megaparsecs away
example.text: Roughly the distance of the Coma Cluster, with $H_0 = 67.4$ km/s/Mpc (Planck 2018).

answer.text: km/s (z ≈ 0.022); the Hubble time is 14.5 billion years.

plot.caption: Velocity against distance for your H₀ (bright) and for the Planck and SH0ES values.

equations.title: Cosmological redshift and scale factor

legend.desc: Scale factor: size of the Universe then, relative to today ($a_0 = 1$)

equations.meaning: Cosmological redshift is not a Doppler shift through space: the wavelength of light stretches in step with space itself while it travels. A galaxy at $z = 10$ sent its light when every distance in the Universe was 11 times smaller. This is why the James Webb Space Telescope observes in the infrared: the ultraviolet light of the first galaxies arrives stretched.

example.title: Galaxy GN-z11
example.text: Spectroscopic redshift $z = 10.60$. Its hydrogen Lyman-alpha line is emitted at 121.567 nm (ultraviolet).

answer.text: nm (1.41 µm, near-infrared); the Universe was 8.6 % of its present size.

plot.caption: Observed wavelength against redshift; the band is visible light.

refs.label: NASA Science — What is Cosmological Redshift?

equations.title: Friedmann equation
equations.latex: \begin{aligned} H^2 &= \frac{8\pi G}{3}\rho - \frac{k c^2}{a^2} + \frac{\Lambda c^2}{3}\\ H(z) &= H_0\sqrt{\Omega_r(1+z)^4 + \Omega_m(1+z)^3 + \Omega_k(1+z)^2 + \Omega_\Lambda}\end{aligned}

legend.desc: Today's radiation, matter and dark-energy densities as fractions of critical ($\Omega_r \approx 9.2\times10^{-5}$ fixed here)

equations.meaning: Alexander Friedmann derived this from general relativity in 1922. It is the energy budget of the expanding Universe: the expansion rate is set by what the Universe contains. Because radiation dilutes as $(1+z)^4$, matter as $(1+z)^3$ and dark energy not at all, each dominated in turn — radiation first, then matter, and now dark energy, which is making the expansion speed up.

example.title: The expansion rate when the Universe was half its size

answer.text: km/s/Mpc — the Universe was expanding almost twice as fast (in this sense) 7.9 billion years ago.

plot.caption: Expansion rate against redshift for your cosmology.

equations.title: Critical density

legend.desc: Density that makes the Universe spatially flat

equations.meaning: Set curvature and dark energy to zero in the Friedmann equation and solve for the density: that is the critical density, the dividing line between a Universe that would recollapse and one that expands forever. Cosmologists quote everything as a fraction of it ($\Omega = \rho/\rho_c$). Observations say the total is within a fraction of a per cent of 1: space is flat.

example.title: Critical density today

answer.text: kg/m³ — about 5 hydrogen atoms per cubic metre, emptier than any laboratory vacuum.

plot.caption: Critical density grows as H².

equations.title: Temperature of the cosmic microwave background

legend.desc: Temperature of the background radiation at redshift $z$

equations.meaning: The cosmic microwave background (CMB) is light from when the Universe first became transparent. Expansion stretches each photon's wavelength by $(1+z)$, and a stretched blackbody stays a blackbody with its temperature divided by $(1+z)$. Run it backwards and at $z \approx 1\,090$ the Universe was about 3 000 K — hot enough to keep hydrogen ionised, which is exactly when it cleared.

example.title: Temperature at recombination

answer.text: K — the glow of a red dwarf's surface, filling all of space.

plot.caption: Background temperature against redshift.

refs.label: Fixsen (2009), The Temperature of the Cosmic Microwave Background
